cim: Clinicians Rate Artificial Intelligence Summaries of Responsive Neurostimulation Data Favorably in Study
cim_eredeti: Clinicians Rate Artificial Intelligence Summaries of Responsive Neurostimulation Data Favorably in Study
szoveg_eredeti:
Clinicians Rate Artificial Intelligence Summaries of Responsive Neurostimulation Data Favorably in Study

In an exploratory single-center investigation, clinical evaluators awarded favorable qualitative ratings to artificial intelligence systems designed to translate complex electronic data from responsive neurostimulation implants into interpretable clinical summaries. Responsive neurostimulation systems manufactured by NeuroPace are approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration as an adjunctive intervention for carefully selected adult individuals presenting with drug-resistant epilepsy, specifically those with one or two localized epileptogenic seizure foci who are not candidates for curative surgical resection. These implanted medical devices monitor brain electrophysiology continuously and log extensive longitudinal intracranial electrocorticography recordings along with detailed stimulation and device-programming parameters. These data streams are transferred wirelessly to the proprietary Patient Data Management System repository. While this secure archive captures an exhaustive longitudinal record of electrographic detections, therapy deliveries, and physician setting adjustments, the resulting reports are dense and technically intricate, demanding substantial time and subspecialty expertise from epileptologists to synthesize into clear, billable clinical notes across routine consultations.

The clinical challenge of interpreting and communicating responsive neurostimulation data extends across multidisciplinary health care teams who interact with these patients outside specialized epilepsy monitoring units. Patients implanted with responsive neurostimulators regularly require medical care from general emergency physicians during acute seizure exacerbations, as well as inpatient hospitalists, consultation-liaison psychiatrists, sleep medicine specialists, advanced practice providers, nursing personnel, and resident trainees. In urgent care environments or evaluations for psychiatric comorbidities such as major depression, treating medical providers frequently require immediate clarity regarding recent objective seizure counts, longitudinal device detection trends, and historical stimulation adjustments. However, device-derived documentation is seldom available in concise formats accessible to nonspecialists, forcing clinicians to navigate lengthy tabular summaries. Consequently, the manual conversion of raw device logs into comprehensive clinical summaries consumes substantial physician time, adding to documentation workload and creating administrative bottlenecks within comprehensive epilepsy management centers.

To address this clinical documentation bottleneck, investigators from the University of Minnesota, Mayo Clinic Rochester, the University of Alabama at Birmingham, and the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston constructed and assessed an automated two-stage computational summarization framework. The study team collected retrospective Patient Data Management System reports from an institutional convenience cohort of fifty patients treated with the NeuroPace responsive neurostimulation system at the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston between January 2015 and December 2023. This cohort incorporated all active adult patients whose electronic device records were accessible to the research team without applying additional clinical inclusion or exclusion filters. Because comprehensive human evaluation across complete patient histories required significant clinical effort from reviewing physicians, researchers generated a computer-randomized representative sample of thirty patients for visit-level evaluation and selected a nested ten-patient subset for longitudinal evolutionary summary assessment.

The engineering workflow constructed by the research group separated the transformation of device records into a two-stage sequential process comprising programmatic data extraction followed by natural language summarization. In the initial data processing stage, portable document format reports downloaded from the Patient Data Management System were parsed programmatically in the Python programming language. Tabular sections containing device configurations and diagnostic tallies were extracted using the open-source Camelot package, with every extracted tabular field manually checked and verified against source clinical records to ensure numerical fidelity. For every clinical follow-up encounter following original surgical device implantation, the extraction algorithm contrasted visit-level programming settings against immediately preceding sessions. This differential comparison identified specific changes in stimulation amplitude, channel configurations, therapy activation states, and diagnostic event tallies, producing structured intermediate metrics that captured chronological changes across consecutive office visits.

In the subsequent summarization stage, the structured visit metrics were converted into natural language narratives through two complementary methods tailored to differing clinical timeframes. First, visit-level records were processed using an explicit rule-based logical script designed to translate technical parameter tables into standard medical terminology describing single clinical encounters. To capture longitudinal disease progression across multiple successive visits, these rule-based encounter summaries were concatenated sequentially and supplied as structured contextual inputs to a locally hosted large language model using an in-context few-shot learning prompt design. The researchers deployed Microsoft Phi-4, an open-weight foundation model containing fourteen billion parameters, executed on an infrastructure consisting of two NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 graphics processing units. Phi-4 was selected over smaller eight-billion-parameter alternatives, including Med42 and DeepSeek-R1-distilled Llama, after internal tests indicated superior narrative consistency and context handling.

The resulting evolutionary summaries synthesized overall longitudinal treatment progression, highlighted meaningful neurostimulator programming adjustments, evaluated the relative clinical effectiveness of distinct electrical stimulation programs, recorded shifts in objective seizure control, documented patient status, and outlined emergent electrographic patterns over time. To rigorously quantify the clinical quality and safety of both summary formats, the investigators recruited a panel of eleven medical evaluators comprising six neurology resident trainees and five board-certified practicing epileptologists. Evaluators reviewed thirty distinct visit-level summaries, assessing each text directly alongside the complete source device report from the Patient Data Management System, which functioned as the factual benchmark. Reviewers recorded ratings using a standardized five-point Likert scale centered on a neutral value of three across six core qualitative dimensions: accuracy, completeness, relevance, coherence, bias, and toxicity.

The survey instrument defined accuracy as the degree to which generated text correctly interpreted therapeutic outcomes and identified optimal stimulation settings, while completeness evaluated whether necessary clinical parameters were retained. Relevance examined clinical usefulness, coherence assessed syntactic flow and logical clarity, bias gauged inappropriate clinical preferences toward specific device settings, and toxicity measured the presence of harmful or misleading language.
